Nunam Iqua|United States of America.f: Nunam Iqua is Yupik for land's end, and the town was called Sheldon Point until residents voted to change it in 1999.

Tuntutuliak|United States of America.f: Tuntutuliak means the land of many caribou in the Yup'ik language.

Pedro Bay|United States of America.f: Pedro Bay's St. Nicholas Chapel is a historic Russian Orthodox church listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Koyuk|United States of America.f: Gold boomtowns Dime Landing and Haycock sprang up near Koyuk around 1914, and coal was mined upriver for steamships and export to Nome.

Selawik|United States of America.f: Selawik comes from the Inupiaq word for place of sheefish.

Scammon Bay|United States of America.f: Scammon Bay was named in 1870 by William Dall for Charles Scammon, marine chief of the Western Union Telegraph Expedition.

Atmautluak|United States of America.f: Atmautluak was founded in the 1960s on high ground above flooding, and dissolved its city government in 1996 for traditional native rule.

Twin Hills|United States of America.f: Twin Hills was not settled until 1965, though it absorbed the older Yupik settlement of Togiagamute, which was in the 1880 census.

Igiugig|United States of America.f: Igiugig means like a throat that swallows water, describing where Lake Iliamna drains into the Kvichak River.

Port Alsworth|United States of America.f: Port Alsworth sits on private land inside Lake Clark National Park and was founded in 1950 by bush pilot and missionary Babe Alsworth.

Kivalina|United States of America.f: Bodies and artifacts of the Ipiutak culture, a pre-Thule people who vanished over a thousand years ago, were found at Kivalina in 2009.

White Mountain|United States of America.f: White Mountain is the only Seward Peninsula village not on the ocean, and Iditarod mushers must rest eight hours here, 77 miles from Nome.

Chenega|United States of America.f: The 1964 Good Friday tsunami killed 26 of the 68 residents of old Chenega and leveled every building except the school and one house.

Kasigluk|United States of America.f: Kasigluk and neighboring Nunapitchuk were merged into one city called Akolmiut in 1969 and split apart again in 1982.

Brevig Mission|United States of America.f: In 1918 the flu killed 72 of Brevig Mission's 80 residents in five days, and a 1997 exhumation there yielded RNA from frozen lung tissue.

Teller|United States of America.f: Teller began as a reindeer station named in 1892 for Senator Henry Teller, and had about 5,000 people during the mining boom.

Circle|United States of America.f: Circle got its name from miners who wrongly thought it sat on the Arctic Circle, which is actually about 50 miles north.

Lopez Island|United States of America.f: Lopez Island has a longstanding custom of waving at every driver, cyclist and pedestrian on its roads.

Goodnews|United States of America.f: Platinum was discovered near Goodnews Bay in 1926 and mined there until 1979.

Chignik Lake|United States of America.f: In 2009 US Marine engineers began building a road to link Chignik Lake with Chignik Lagoon.

Central|United States of America.f: Every February Central hosts a checkpoint of the Yukon Quest sled dog race, with the Steese Roadhouse as a midway stop.

Old Harbor|United States of America.f: In 1784 Grigory Shelikhov and 130 Russian fur traders massacred several hundred Sugpiat at Refuge Rock, an event called the Awa'uq Massacre.

Kalaupapa|United States of America.f: More than 8,500 people diagnosed with leprosy were exiled to Kalaupapa by the Hawaiian government and legally declared dead.

Larsen Bay|United States of America.f: Larsen Bay is named for Peter Adolf Larsen, a Danish immigrant who worked there as a hunter and sailor.

Stony River|United States of America.f: Stony River is where Yup'ik Eskimos meet three Athabaskan peoples, the Deg Hit'an, Dena'ina and Upper Kuskokwim.

Chignik|United States of America.f: Benny Benson, who designed the Alaska state flag, was born in Chignik in 1913.

Decatur (WA)|United States of America.f: Decatur Island, named by the Wilkes Expedition in 1841 for Stephen Decatur, has no ferry service and only 71 residents.

Tok|United States of America.f: Tok began in 1942 as an Alaska Highway road camp nicknamed Million Dollar Camp, and a 1990 fire stopped just short of its first building.

Block Island|United States of America.f: Block Island is named for Dutch explorer Adriaen Block, who charted it in 1614, and about 40 percent of it is protected conservation land.

Chicken|United States of America.f: Chicken likely took its name from a creek whose gold was the size of chicken feed, and the 2020 census counted just 12 residents.

Nunapitchuk|United States of America.f: Nunapitchuk has no roads, and its buildings are linked by boardwalks across the tundra.

Kongiganak|United States of America.f: The current Kongiganak was settled in the 1960s by people from Kwigillingok seeking higher ground to escape floods.

Kelleys Island|United States of America.f: Kelleys Island preserves the largest exposure of glacial grooves, carved by ice-age glaciers into a depression about 9 meters wide.

Blakely Island|United States of America.f: Blakely Island has no public ferry, and was named by Charles Wilkes for Johnston Blakeley, a naval commander in the War of 1812.

Port Lions|United States of America.f: Port Lions was built to house survivors of two villages destroyed by the 1964 earthquake and named for the Lions Club that helped.

False Pass|United States of America.f: False Pass was named for a strait once thought impassable to deep-draft ships, and only 35 of its 397 residents live there year-round.

Minto|United States of America.f: Minto means among the lakes in Lower Tanana, and its 250 people include the last first-language speakers of that Athabaskan tongue.
